terms.definition: a model built from many small calculating units (neurons) arranged in layers; each layer's outputs are the next layer's inputs.
one step of a network: a group of neurons that all read the same inputs and pass their outputs on together.
one calculating unit: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the sum through an activation function.
a number on one connection between two neurons; the input is multiplied by it. Training is changing the weights.
a layer in which every neuron is wired to every input (written Dense in code). Also called a dense layer; not Chapter 2's 'dense' (the opposite of a sparse matrix).
one dot of a picture: one number (grey) or three numbers (red, green, blue) at one row and column.
a CNN: a neural network whose early layers are convolutional layers (and usually pooling layers) instead of fully connected ones.
the small patch of the layer below (or of the image) that one neuron reads, e.g. 3 x 3 pixels.
the same small set of weights is reused at every position of the image, instead of a separate set per pixel.
a layer that slides small grids of weights over its input and writes one number per position; in code, Conv2D.
a layer with no weights that shrinks its input grid by keeping one number (the max or the mean) per small window (lesson b06).
the S-shaped function 1 / (1 + e^-z): squeezes any number into 0..1.
the small function a neuron applies to its total before passing it on (for example the S-shaped sigmoid). Without one, a stack of layers could only learn straight-line rules.
the narrow part that limits the whole: in a network, a layer with fewer outputs than it gets inputs.
a small grid of weights (e.g. 7 x 7) slid across the image; it responds strongly where the image looks like its pattern.
in this chapter, another name for a filter (kernel_size = its height and width). Not the similarity kernel of Chapter 2.
the 2D grid of outputs one filter produces by sliding over its input: big numbers where its pattern is, small ones elsewhere.
extra zeros added around the border of the input so the filter can also be centred on edge pixels (padding="same" in code; "valid" = no padding).
how many pixels the filter (or pooling window) moves between two neighbouring outputs; stride 2 roughly halves the height and width.
lay the rows of a grid end to end as one long list; the Flatten layer does this before a dense layer.
produce a smaller grid than you started with (by a stride or a pooling layer).
one 2D layer of a picture or of a layer's output: an RGB image has 3 channels, a layer with 32 filters outputs 32 (feature maps).
red, green, blue: a colour image stored as three channels, one per colour, each 0 to 255.
one extra number a neuron adds to its inputs-times-weights total; a convolutional layer has one per filter, like a brightness knob for that filter's output.
one output number of a neuron for one input image; a layer's whole output grid is its activations.
each input times its weight, all added up (plus the bias): what a neuron computes before its activation function.
Google's library for deep learning: fast arithmetic on big grids of numbers.
the part of TensorFlow for building and training networks with ready-made layers (imports start with tf.keras).
TensorFlow's array: a number, a list, a table or a stack of tables, all of one type; images come as [batch, height, width, channels].
a small group of images processed together in one step (32 by default).
a layer you write yourself as a Python class that inherits from tf.keras.layers.Layer: __init__ builds its parts, call() computes.
graphics processor: a chip that does a network's arithmetic much faster than the ordinary processor, with its own (limited) memory.
the computer's ordinary processor.
the computer's working memory, where the numbers being computed are held.
running the input through the network from the first layer to the last to get a prediction.
the method that computes every weight's gradient by walking backward from the loss through the layers, one layer at a time.
for every weight, one number saying how much the loss would change if that weight moved a little, and in which direction.
using a trained network to predict, with no weight changes (predict() in code).
one update of all the weights, computed from one batch.
the usual number format: 32 bits = 4 bytes per number; 16-bit floats take half the memory and are less precise.
the crash you get when the numbers a step needs do not fit in RAM (or GPU memory).
pooling that keeps the largest value in each window (e.g. 2 x 2, stride 2): three of every four numbers are dropped.
the output stays the same when the input is shifted a little ('translation' = a shift in position).
shift the input and the output shifts the same way; what pixel-level tasks need.
giving every pixel of an image a class (road, car, sky ...); objects of the same class are not told apart.
pooling that keeps the mean of each window instead of the max.
max pooling across groups of feature maps (channels) at the same pixel, instead of across a window of pixels.
the mean of each entire feature map: one number per map per image; [2, 28, 28, 3] becomes (2, 3).
a Keras layer that just wraps a function you give it (Lambda(lambda X: ...)); it has no weights.
the rectified linear unit, max(0, z): keeps positive numbers, turns negative ones into 0.
an output activation that turns the final scores into probabilities adding up to 1, one per class.
during training, randomly ignore a share of a layer's neurons (50% here) at each step, so no neuron becomes indispensable; switched off for predictions.
the book's image set: 70,000 greyscale 28 x 28 photos of clothes in 10 classes.
Keras's simplest kind of model: a plain list of layers, each feeding the next.
one full pass over the training set.
the share of images whose predicted class is the true class, e.g. 0.92 = 92% right.
one number saying how wrong the network's predictions are; training pushes it down.
a public set of over a million photos in 1,000 classes; its yearly contest (ILSVRC) is where most architectures in this chapter were first shown.
the share of images whose true class is NOT among the model's five best guesses.
making extra training images by slightly shifting, flipping, rotating or re-lighting the ones you have.
AlexNet's step that divides a neuron's output by how strongly the same pixel fires in neighbouring feature maps, so the maps compete.
in LRN, how many neighbouring feature maps above and below take part (r).
GoogLeNet's block: 1 x 1, 3 x 3 and 5 x 5 convolutions and a pooling layer run side by side on the same input, their outputs stacked along the depth.
a convolution whose filter reads one pixel but all channels: a learned mix of the channels, applied at every position.
a layer (usually a 1 x 1 convolution) that outputs fewer feature maps than it reads, to cut the cost of the next layer.
gluing tensors together along one axis; 'depth concatenation' stacks feature maps of the same height and width.
a wire that adds a block's input straight onto its output, so the block only has to learn the difference.
one ResNet block: two (or three) convolutional layers with a skip connection around them.
the difference between what a block must output and its input: f(x) = h(x) - x.
gradients that shrink layer after layer on the way back, so the first layers get almost no update and stop learning.
the do-nothing function: it returns its input unchanged.
a layer that re-centres and re-scales each channel using the current batch's statistics, which keeps very deep networks trainable.
Residual Network (2015): a very deep CNN whose blocks add their input back onto their output (lesson b11); ResNet-34, -50, -152 differ in depth.
a convolution split in two: one spatial filter per input channel, then 1 x 1 filters that mix the channels. Fewer weights, less arithmetic.
Extreme Inception (2016): a CNN built almost entirely from depthwise separable convolutions; reused for flower photos in lesson b18.
a small add-on block that averages each feature map, passes the averages through two dense layers, and multiplies every map by the weight (0 to 1) that comes back.
a short list of numbers standing in for something bigger (a set of maps, an object's appearance).
a CNN family (B0 to B7) that grows depth, width and input size together by fixed factors.
grow depth by alpha^phi, width by beta^phi and resolution by gamma^phi together, with alpha x beta^2 x gamma^2 about 2.
how often the model's single best guess is the right class.
the wait for one answer.
a small, fast CNN designed for phones (3.5 million parameters).
an architecture shipped together with weights someone already trained, usually on ImageNet.
each pretrained Keras model's own function that rescales pixels (0-255) to the range that model was trained on.
turns a model's 1,000 ImageNet scores into (class id, name, probability) triples.
reusing the lower layers of a network trained on a big task (e.g. ImageNet) for a new task with little data.
the top of a network: the layers that turn features into the final answer (here the pooling and dense output layers).
set layer.trainable = False: the layer still computes, but training no longer changes its weights.
in this chapter: continue training some of a pretrained network's own layers, gently (small learning rate), after the new head has settled.
the size of each training step: weight change = learning rate x gradient.
the object that turns gradients into weight updates (SGD = stochastic gradient descent); chosen in compile().
an optimizer setting that keeps part of the previous step's direction (0.9 = 90%), which smooths the path.
Keras's step that attaches a loss, an optimizer and metrics to a model, before fit().
a free set of 3,670 flower photos in 5 classes (dandelion, daisy, tulips, sunflowers, roses), loaded with TensorFlow Datasets.
the rectangle around an object, given as 4 numbers (here centre x, centre y, width, height, each 0 to 1).
saying where the object is (a bounding box), not only what it is.
the usual classification loss: minus the log of the probability given to the true class.
mean squared error: average of the squared differences between predicted and true numbers.
intersection over union: the area where two boxes overlap divided by the area they cover together; 1 = identical, 0 = no overlap.
finding every object in an image: a class and a bounding box for each.
the model's estimated probability that an object is centred in this window or cell (one sigmoid unit).
the cleanup that keeps the highest-objectness box and drops the boxes overlapping it by more than an IoU threshold, then repeats.
a network made only of convolutional and pooling layers (no dense layer), so it accepts any image size.
You Only Look Once: a detector that predicts every box and class for a grid of cells in one forward pass.
a classic method that predicts where a moving object should be now from where it has been, assuming constant velocity.
a classic method that finds the cheapest overall pairing between two lists (detections and tracks) given a cost for every pair.
producing a bigger grid than you were given.
an upsampling layer: it spreads its input out with zeros, then convolves with learned weights; a bigger stride gives a bigger output.
a convolution with gaps in its filter (dilation_rate): a wider view for the same number of weights.
segmentation that also tells objects of the same class apart (each bicycle separately).

the Keras style that builds a model by calling layers on tensors, x = layer(x), then naming the first and last tensors in tf.keras.Model(inputs=..., outputs=...), instead of listing layers in Sequential.
the GPU's own memory, separate from the computer's RAM; the model, its activations and a batch must all fit in it during training.
70,000 grey 28 x 28 images of handwritten digits 0-9 (60,000 for training, 10,000 for testing) — the older set that Fashion MNIST was made to replace.
repainting one photo in the style of another (say, a painting) by adjusting its pixels until a pretrained CNN's feature maps match the photo's content and the painting's textures.
